title: LIME
text:
Preface
A fitted model can predict accurately while giving little indication of how it reached one particular prediction. This is common with random forests, gradient boosted trees, support vector machines, and neural networks. It matters in biological work because a prediction about one tumour, patient, or cell is often followed immediately by a second question: which measurements made the model behave this way for this sample?
LIME, short for Local Interpretable Model Agnostic Explanations, answers that question by studying the fitted model close to one observation. It creates artificial observations, obtains predictions from the original model, and fits a simpler model that approximates those predictions nearby. The result is an explanation of the fitted model’s local behaviour. It is not a model of the biological mechanism and it is not automatically a statement about the population as a whole.
Start with Understanding LIME.

title: LIME
text:
Primary sources
The module follows the original paper by Ribeiro, Singh, and Guestrin, “Why Should I Trust You?”: Explaining the Predictions of Any Classifier, and checks current behaviour against the Python repository and documentation, the R lime reference, and the LIME chapter of Christoph Molnar’s Interpretable Machine Learning. Package behaviour described in the practical chapter was verified with Python lime 0.2.0.1 and R lime 0.5.4.

title: 1  Understanding LIME
text:
1.1 One difficult prediction
Suppose a gradient boosted tree has been trained to classify tumour samples. Its inputs include two biomarkers, an inflammatory marker, age, and several laboratory measurements. For patient A it reports a probability of malignancy of 0.82.
The number is useful, but it does not tell us what the fitted model was doing around this patient. Did the prediction depend mainly on biomarker A? Did biomarker B push in the opposite direction? Would a small change in the inflammatory marker alter the prediction, or is the model almost flat there?
These questions concern one observation. They differ from asking which features matter most on average across the entire dataset. LIME is a local explanation method. It does not replace the fitted model. It constructs a simple local surrogate model that behaves similarly to the fitted model near the observation being explained.

title: 1  Understanding LIME
text:
1.2 Local is not global
A nonlinear model can be pictured as a curved prediction surface. Every position on the surface represents a combination of two biomarker values. Colour represents the model’s predicted disease probability.







Figure 1.1: The complete nonlinear prediction surface and a magnified neighborhood around patient A. Black contours in the local panel come from a linear surrogate fitted only near that patient.




The left panel of Figure 1.1 shows the whole fitted surface. No single plane can reproduce all its bends. The circle selects a small region around patient A. In the right panel, straight contour lines approximate the surface within that region. Those lines would be wrong in much of the left panel, but global accuracy is not their job.
This distinction is the basis of LIME. The original model may be highly nonlinear. A linear surrogate can still be useful when it only has to describe a small neighborhood. A local explanation should never be promoted silently into a global claim.

title: 1  Understanding LIME
text:
1.3 The LIME process
The method can be followed as six connected stages.







Figure 1.2: The six stages of tabular LIME. LIME selects an observation, generates artificial observations, obtains black-box probabilities, weights observations by proximity, and fits a local surrogate.




1. Choose an observation. Patient A has a fixed set of measured values and a black-box probability of 0.82. LIME explains this prediction, not every prediction made by the model.
2. Generate modified observations. LIME creates many artificial rows by changing the feature values. These rows are probes. They let us ask how the fitted model behaves when its inputs vary. They are not newly observed patients.
3. Obtain predictions from the original model. Every artificial row is sent through the already fitted model. LIME uses the model’s output, not the true disease status of these artificial observations.

For classification, the useful output is usually a predicted probability for one class. For regression, it is the fitted numerical response. The artificial rows have no observed outcomes, so class labels such as malignant and benign cannot be the response of the surrogate.
4. Give nearby observations more influence. An artificial observation very similar to patient A is more relevant to the local question than one far away. LIME therefore gives nearby rows large weights and distant rows small weights. Point size in the lower-left panel of Figure 1.2 represents this influence.
5. Fit a simple model. For tabular LIME, the surrogate is commonly a sparse weighted linear regression. Its response consists of probabilities such as 0.61, 0.73, 0.82, and 0.87. It is not fitted to zero-one disease outcomes. This is why a linear regression appears inside a classification explanation: it approximates the classifier’s probability surface.
6. Interpret the local surrogate. The surrogate assigns a weight to each selected feature. The sign indicates which direction the feature moves the surrogate’s prediction for the chosen class. The magnitude describes its influence in this particular local approximation.







Figure 1.3: A typical LIME feature plot for the malignant class. Positive local weights support the selected class and negative weights push against it.




In Figure 1.3, high biomarker A and low biomarker B support the model’s malignant prediction. Age has little influence in this neighborhood. These weights are not coefficients from the original boosted tree. They are not causal effects. They describe a separate simple model fitted to mimic the original model around patient A.

title: 1  Understanding LIME
section: 1.4 Why a linear surrogate can describe a nonlinear model
text:
1.4 Why a linear surrogate can describe a nonlinear model
The word linear describes the surrogate, not the original model. A small portion of a curved probability function can often be approximated by a line. Move to another part of the curve and a different line is needed.







Figure 1.4: Three local linear approximations at different positions on one nonlinear probability curve.




The three colored lines in Figure 1.4 all explain the same black-box model. The left explanation is almost flat. The middle one has a steep positive slope. The right one rises more gently. None is a contradiction. Each describes a different local region.
This argument has a limit. Some neighborhoods contain sharp thresholds, several interacting boundaries, or other behaviour that a plane cannot reproduce. LIME can still return coefficients in that situation. The existence of coefficients does not prove that the local surrogate is faithful. Its fit must be checked.

title: 1  Understanding LIME
section: 1.5 Different observations can have different explanations
text:
1.5 Different observations can have different explanations
Because the fitted surface changes from place to place, two samples can have different explanations even when their predicted probabilities are similar. Biomarker A may receive a positive local weight for one sample, a small weight for another, and a negative weight where the surface bends back. The corresponding value for biomarker B can change at the same time because the model contains an interaction.
A LIME weight therefore belongs to a feature, an observation, a selected class, a perturbation procedure, and a neighborhood definition together. Removing any of that context changes what the number means.

title: 1  Understanding LIME
section: 1.6 Near and far from a decision boundary
text:
1.6 Near and far from a decision boundary
The location of the observation also affects how informative a local explanation can be.







Figure 1.5: Artificial observations near a changing decision boundary and in a flat high-probability region.




Near the boundary in the left panel of Figure 1.5, small changes in the biomarker produce a wide range of model probabilities. The surrogate can estimate a clear local direction. Deep inside the predicted class in the right panel, almost every artificial observation receives a probability near one. A nearly flat explanation is accurate there, but it says little about what would eventually make the prediction cross the boundary. LIME describes the model near the point. It does not automatically search for the nearest way to change the decision.

title: 1  Understanding LIME
text:
1.7 What model agnostic means
LIME needs a route from inputs to predictions:

input data → fitted model → predicted probability or numerical response

It does not need the model’s tree splits, coefficients, gradients, neural network weights, or training algorithm. The same general procedure can therefore probe XGBoost, random forests, support vector machines, and neural networks. This is the meaning of model agnostic.
The prediction function still matters. A classifier must return probabilities with columns in a known class order. A preprocessing pipeline must apply exactly the same transformations during explanation as it did during model fitting. Model agnostic does not mean interface agnostic.

title: 1  Understanding LIME
text:
1.8 Sparse explanations and fidelity
A local linear model with 100 displayed coefficients is rarely a useful explanation. LIME usually selects a small number of features or the user requests a maximum number. This creates a tradeoff.

Fewer features make the explanation shorter and easier to communicate.
More features may reproduce the black-box predictions more accurately in the chosen neighborhood.

The degree to which the surrogate reproduces the original model nearby is called local fidelity. A five-feature explanation with strong local fidelity may be useful. A three-feature explanation with poor fidelity is simple but misleading. The practical chapter shows how both R and Python report a local score.

title: 1  Understanding LIME
text:
1.9 Classification, multiclass models, and regression
For binary classification, LIME approximates the predicted probability for a selected class. An explanation for malignancy says which local features support or oppose the model’s malignancy probability.
For multiclass classification, an explanation is attached to one class at a time. A gene-expression profile may be classified as one of several cell types. Features supporting the T-cell probability need not be the same as those opposing the B-cell probability. Software may default to the most probable class or to a numerical label, so the class must be checked explicitly.
For regression, the target is the model’s numerical prediction. A model might predict a cytokine concentration, tumour volume, or continuous drug response. LIME fits the same kind of local surrogate to those predicted numbers.

title: 1  Understanding LIME
text:
1.10 Interpretable representations
The black box and the explanation do not always use the same representation. LIME calls the human-facing version the interpretable representation.
For tabular data, a continuous measurement can be displayed as a condition such as biomarker_A > 2.3 even though the fitted model received a numerical value. For text, interpretable features commonly indicate whether words or tokens are present. Artificial documents are made by hiding tokens. For images, interpretable features are usually connected regions called superpixels. Artificial images are made by masking selected superpixels.
This module focuses on tabular biological data. Text and image LIME use the same broad logic, but their perturbations, distances, and interpretable features are different.

title: 1  Understanding LIME
text:
1.11 Questions answered by related methods
Several model interpretation methods produce feature-based plots. Their questions are different.







Method
Main question




LIME
What simple model approximates the fitted model around this observation?


SHAP
How can the difference between a baseline prediction and this prediction be attributed among features?


Permutation importance
How much predictive performance is lost when information in a feature is disrupted?


Counterfactual explanation
What change to the predictors could change the prediction?


Global surrogate model
What simple model approximates the black box over a broad portion of the data?



LIME and SHAP bar charts can look similar, but LIME weights are coefficients from a sampled local surrogate. SHAP values are feature attributions relative to a baseline under a Shapley-value definition. Neither plot should be interpreted from appearance alone.

title: 1  Understanding LIME
text:
1.12 When LIME is useful
LIME is useful when the aim is to understand individual predictions from a complicated model. It can help check whether a model uses biologically sensible variables for a particular sample, investigate an unusual or incorrect prediction, compare local behaviour across patients, and communicate one prediction with a small set of features. It is also useful when the model can only be accessed through a prediction function.
LIME can support model debugging. If laboratory batch indicators repeatedly dominate individual explanations, the fitted model may have learned an unwanted shortcut. That observation is a reason to investigate the data and model. It is not evidence that LIME itself has corrected the problem.

title: 1  Understanding LIME
section: 1.13 When LIME should be used carefully
text:
1.13 When LIME should be used carefully

1.13.1 A local explanation is not global importance
A feature that matters near one patient may be unimportant across most patients. Conversely, a globally important feature can have little effect in a flat local region. Many local explanations can be summarized, but one explanation alone cannot establish population-wide importance.


1.13.2 The neighborhood is chosen by the algorithm
The definition of nearby is not given by nature. It depends on feature scaling, distance, kernel width, discretization, and sampling. Changing those choices can change the explanation.







Figure 1.6: Three locality kernels. A narrow width concentrates influence close to the observation, while a wide width lets distant perturbations influence the surrogate.




The narrow curve in Figure 1.6 asks a very local question. The wide curve asks the surrogate to cover a broader region. Neither is universally correct. The width must be judged in the context of the data and the local fit.


1.13.3 Artificial observations may be unrealistic
Biological predictors often move together. If two biomarkers are tightly correlated, sampling them independently can create combinations that are rare or impossible in real samples.







Figure 1.7: Observed correlated biomarkers and independently generated perturbations. Many artificial observations lie outside the narrow region occupied by the real data.




In Figure 1.7, the fitted model is queried well outside the observed data manifold. Its predictions there may be arbitrary extrapolations. LIME then learns from those predictions. The problem should be inspected rather than assumed away.


1.13.4 Correlated features can share or exchange attribution
When two features carry similar information, several local linear models may fit almost equally well. Feature selection may choose biomarker A in one run and its correlated partner in another. A coefficient can also change when the partner is included or removed. This is familiar from regression, but LIME adds random sampling and local weighting to the problem.


1.13.5 Sampling introduces variability
LIME’s artificial neighborhood is random. Repeated runs can produce different selected features and weights.







Figure 1.8: Local weights from repeated explanations with different random seeds. Correlated biomarkers exchange some weight and all estimates vary.




Setting a random seed makes one run reproducible. It does not remove the underlying sensitivity. Repeating an explanation is a direct way to measure it.


1.13.6 Poor local fidelity weakens the explanation







Figure 1.9: A high-fidelity linear surrogate and a poor linear surrogate fitted to complicated local behavior.




The right panel of Figure 1.9 still has a fitted line and coefficients. They should not be interpreted strongly because the line does not reproduce the black-box outputs. Fidelity is an essential diagnostic, not an optional decoration.


1.13.7 High-dimensional biological data needs additional care
Gene expression, methylation, and proteomics datasets can contain thousands of correlated predictors. In high dimensions, distances become less discriminating, sparse feature selection becomes unstable, and independently generated rows can move far from the biological manifold. Computation also grows because every perturbation must be passed through the model.
LIME is not automatically invalid for omics data. It does require stronger checks. Useful options include explaining a biologically meaningful lower-dimensional representation, grouping related variables, using a perturbation generator suited to the data, checking stability across seeds and locality settings, and comparing the result with another interpretation method. If a model was trained on transformed components, explaining the raw genes requires a prediction pipeline that performs the transformation. A label attached to a transformed component should not be presented as if it were a measured gene.

title: 1  Understanding LIME
text:
1.14 Conceptual summary
LIME creates artificial observations, asks the fitted model to predict them, gives nearby observations more influence, and fits an interpretable local surrogate to the resulting model outputs. For classification, those outputs are usually class probabilities. The surrogate may be linear even when the fitted model is nonlinear because it is intended to work only nearby.
The explanation belongs to one observation and one class. It depends on how the neighborhood is sampled and weighted. It describes the fitted model, not a biological cause. Its feature weights should be read only after checking the class, local fidelity, stability, correlated predictors, and the plausibility of the artificial observations.

3.1 Packages and implementation versions
This chapter uses the R package lime 0.5.4 and the original Python package lime 0.2.0.1. The R and Python projects implement the same framework but are not ports of one another. Their defaults differ enough that identical weights should not be expected.
The fitted model is XGBoost. Its role is deliberately small: fit a nonlinear classifier, supply class probabilities, and let LIME probe it. The simulation, split, and selected sample IDs are stored in shared files so both languages begin from the same rows.

3.3 Known truth and fitted surface
The left panel of Figure 3.1 fixes the other predictors at their training medians and shows the known probability as biomarker A and biomarker B vary. The interaction bends the boundary. The right panel shows the XGBoost fit under the same conditions. Its stepped surface is typical of a tree ensemble.







Figure 3.1: The known simulation probability and the probability learned by XGBoost, with all other predictors fixed at their training medians.




Model fitting is kept identical in purpose. Small prediction differences remain because the R and Python XGBoost interfaces and released library versions are not guaranteed to construct byte-for-byte identical ensembles.

RPython


dtrain <- xgb.DMatrix(
  as.matrix(train[, feature_cols]),
  label = train$outcome
)

fit <- xgb.train(
  params = list(
    objective = "binary:logistic",
    eval_metric = "logloss",
    max_depth = 3,
    eta = 0.05,
    subsample = 0.85,
    colsample_bytree = 0.9,
    nthread = 1,
    seed = 2026
  ),
  data = dtrain,
  nrounds = 250,
  verbose = 0
)

test_probability <- predict(fit, as.matrix(test[, feature_cols]))
test_class <- as.integer(test_probability >= 0.5)

auc <- function(y, p) {
  r <- rank(p)
  n1 <- sum(y == 1)
  n0 <- sum(y == 0)
  (sum(r[y == 1]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}

cat("accuracy:", round(mean(test_class == test$outcome), 3), "\n")

text:
3.4 Create a LIME explainer
An explainer stores information about the training predictors and the fitted model. It should receive training rows only. Supplying the test set would leak its distribution into the explanation procedure.

RPython


explainer <- lime(
  x = train[, feature_cols],
  model = fit,
  bin_continuous = TRUE,
  n_bins = 4,
  quantile_bins = TRUE
)
bin_continuous = TRUE is the R default. Each numerical predictor is divided into four quantile bins. The interpretable features indicate whether a value belongs to an interval. With bin_continuous = FALSE, use_density = TRUE samples a numerical feature from a kernel density estimate. Setting use_density = FALSE uses a normal distribution estimated from the training column.


explainer = LimeTabularExplainer(
    training_data=train[feature_cols].to_numpy(),
    mode="classification",
    feature_names=feature_cols,
    class_names=["class 0", "class 1"],
    discretize_continuous=True,
    discretizer="quartile",
    feature_selection="auto",
    random_state=2026,
)
Python also discretizes numerical predictors into quartiles by default. Other built-in discretizers are "decile" and supervised "entropy". If discretization is off, numerical perturbations come from normal distributions using training means and standard deviations. sample_around_instance=True centers those normal draws on the explained row instead of the training mean. That option does not create conditional samples and has no effect on predictors converted to categorical bins.



The class names in Python must follow the order returned by the prediction function. Check it rather than guessing:
print(fit.classes_)                       # [0, 1]
print(fit.predict_proba(cases[feature_cols]).shape)  # three rows, two classes
For this model, probability column 0 is class 0 and column 1 is class 1. The R method for xgb.Booster names its two probability columns "1" and "0". We therefore request label "1" in R and integer label 1 in Python.

3.5 Explain the three observations
The code requests five features and 5,000 perturbations for the class 1 probability. One class is explained per call so there is no ambiguity about the reported fidelity score.

set.seed(2026)
explanations <- explain(
  x = cases[, feature_cols],
  explainer = explainer,
  labels = "1",
  n_features = 5,
  n_permutations = 5000,
  feature_select = "auto",
  dist_fun = "gower"
)

suppressWarnings(plot_features(explanations))




R lime feature plots for the three selected observations.





python_explanations = {}

for _, row in cases.iterrows():
    explanation = explainer.explain_instance(
        data_row=row[feature_cols].to_numpy(dtype=float),
        predict_fn=fit.predict_proba,
        labels=(1,),
        num_features=5,
        num_samples=5000,
        distance_metric="euclidean",
    )
    python_explanations[row["sample_id"]] = explanation
    explanation.as_pyplot_figure(label=1)
    plt.title(f"{row['case_type']}: class 1")
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()




Python LIME explanations for the same observations. Each panel also reports the black-box probability, local prediction, and local R-squared.






Read each plot in local, class-specific language. A positive weight supports class 1 in the surrogate fitted around that row. A negative weight opposes class 1. An interval such as biomarker_a <= -0.66 is a binary interpretable feature. Its weight is not a per-unit slope of biomarker A.
Comparing the cases with the known surface gives a useful check. Biomarker A and biomarker B should usually appear because the true probability depends strongly on them. Inflammation and age may appear with smaller weights. A noise feature can still appear because XGBoost fitted a finite noisy sample and LIME fitted another finite artificial sample. Neither procedure knows the data-generating equation.

text:
3.6 Inspect the explanation instead of only plotting it

3.6.1 R output fields
explain() returns one row per selected feature, with explanation-level values repeated down those rows.
explanations[, c(
  "case", "label", "label_prob", "model_r2",
  "model_prediction", "model_intercept", "feature",
  "feature_value", "feature_weight", "feature_desc"
)]
case  label_prob  model_r2  model_prediction  feature
1        0.616      0.279        0.210         biomarker_a
2        0.038      0.329        0.061         biomarker_a
3        0.936      0.484        0.515         biomarker_a

Five feature rows are returned per case. Explanation-level values repeat.

prediction contains the original model probabilities for all classes.
data contains the original row being explained.
label is the class being explained and label_prob is the black-box probability for that class.
feature is the original column name. feature_value is its value in the explained row. feature_desc is the human-readable bin or condition.
feature_weight is the coefficient in the local ridge regression.
model_intercept and model_prediction belong to the local surrogate. model_prediction should be compared with label_prob, but they need not be equal.
model_r2 is the weighted coefficient of determination on the artificial neighborhood. Values closer to one indicate that the selected local model reproduces more of the variation in black-box probabilities. A low value warns that the coefficients are a weak summary of that neighborhood.

The first artificial row is the observation being explained. Its black-box probability can differ substantially from model_prediction even when the overall weighted fit is moderate. Inspect both the pointwise difference and model_r2.


3.6.2 Python attributes
row_id = cases.loc[cases["case_type"] == "near boundary", "sample_id"].iloc[0]
explanation = python_explanations[row_id]

print("black-box probabilities:", explanation.predict_proba)
print("feature descriptions and weights:", explanation.as_list(label=1))
print("raw feature map:", explanation.as_map()[1])
print("local prediction:", float(explanation.local_pred[0]))
print("local weighted R-squared:", float(explanation.score))
print("local intercept:", float(explanation.intercept[1]))

feature descriptions and weights:
  biomarker_a <= -0.66              -0.357
  inflammation > 0.71                0.087
  -0.69 < biomarker_b <= -0.03       0.068
  56.85 < age <= 64.73               0.026
  -0.02 < lab_noise_1 <= 0.73        0.012

local weighted R-squared: 0.318

as_list() returns displayed feature descriptions and weights. as_map() returns feature identifiers and weights. local_pred is the surrogate’s prediction at the explained row. score is the weighted local R-squared. The current released package stores one score and one local_pred for the last class fitted, so separate calls are safest when explanations for several classes must be audited.
model_regressor in explain_instance() can replace the default ridge regression. A replacement must expose coef_ and accept sample_weight in its fit() method. It should also implement a meaningful score() because that value becomes the reported local score. Changing the regressor changes the explanation and should be documented. The default ridge model is the appropriate starting point for this chapter.
For multiclass work, pass the intended numerical class in labels, after checking the prediction-column order. top_labels=k instead asks Python LIME to explain the \(k\) classes with the largest probabilities and overrides labels. R offers the parallel choice between explicit labels and n_labels. Explicit labels are preferable when the scientific question names the class in advance.






ImportantA plot is not evidence of a good explanation



Both packages can draw an attractive feature plot when local R-squared is low. Interpret the weights only after checking fidelity and the difference between the local and black-box predictions. A poor surrogate should lead to a changed neighborhood, representation, or surrogate, or to the conclusion that this LIME explanation is inadequate.

3.16 Preprocessing pipelines
LIME must query the exact function used for ordinary prediction. Suppose a model was trained after log transformation, imputation, one-hot encoding, and standardization. Every artificial row must pass through the fitted versions of those steps. Refitting a scaler or imputer on each artificial neighborhood changes the model and is incorrect.
In Python, pass pipeline.predict_proba when a scikit-learn Pipeline begins with preprocessing and accepts original columns. In R, either use a supported fitted workflow or provide predict_model() and model_type() methods whose prediction path applies the stored transformations. Create the LIME explainer from the representation you want to perturb. If the model accepts principal components but the explanation should mention genes, a gene-to-component transformation must sit inside the prediction function. LIME cannot infer that mapping.

title: 2  Using LIME in R and Python
text:
2.17 Practical recommendations

Confirm the class and probability column being explained.
Keep the complete fitted preprocessing path inside the prediction function.
Inspect local R-squared and the local prediction before interpreting weights.
Repeat explanations with several seeds and report unstable feature selection.
Try a small range of defensible locality settings and feature counts.
Check correlated predictors and whether artificial rows are biologically plausible.
Use enough features to achieve useful fidelity, but few enough to keep the explanation readable.
Prefer held-out observations when teaching or auditing predictive behaviour.
Do not turn one local explanation into global importance or a causal statement.
Treat LIME as one source of evidence about model behaviour rather than ground truth about the biological system.

2.18 Summary
Correct use of LIME requires more than calling plot_features() or as_list(). The model output, class order, perturbation distribution, representation, distance, locality rule, feature selection, and random seed all help define the explanation. title: 3  How LIME works
text:
3.1 Begin with an already fitted prediction function
Let the fitted prediction function be denoted by
\[\hat f.\]
The hat is a reminder that the function has already been estimated from training data. LIME begins after this fitting step. It does not estimate or alter the original model.
Let the observation to be explained be a vector with \(p\) predictors,
\[x_0 = (x_{01},x_{02},\ldots,x_{0p}).\]
For regression, the original model’s prediction at this observation is the numerical value
\[\hat f(x_0).\]
For classification, an explanation must be attached to a class. If \(c\) is the class of interest, define
\[\hat f_c(x_0)
=
P_{\hat f}(Y=c\mid x_0).\]
The notation means the probability assigned to class \(c\) by the fitted model. It is not a claim that the fitted probability is the true biological probability.

title: 3  How LIME works
section: 3.2 The response of the explanation model
text:
3.2 The response of the explanation model
LIME creates a new local modelling problem. Its inputs are artificial observations and its responses are predictions from \(\hat f\). The mapping is
\[Z \longrightarrow \hat f(Z),\]
not
\[Z \longrightarrow Y.\]
For a classifier and class \(c\), the response attached to artificial observation \(z_i\) is
\[y_i^* = \hat f_c(z_i).\]
The star distinguishes this generated response from an outcome observed in nature. It is a continuous value such as 0.72 or 0.91. For regression,
\[y_i^* = \hat f(z_i).\]
This construction resolves an apparent mismatch. A classifier was fitted to class outcomes, yet a linear regression appears inside LIME. The regression is not being fitted to the original class labels. It is approximating a surface of predicted probabilities.

title: 3  How LIME works
text:
3.3 Artificial observations
Generate \(m\) perturbed observations around the explanation problem,
\[z_1,z_2,\ldots,z_m.\]
Each \(z_i\) has \(p\) feature values. The first row in common implementations is \(x_0\) itself. The remaining rows are random modifications.
The word around needs care. It does not necessarily mean that every value was sampled from a distribution centered on \(x_0\). Python LIME without discretization normally draws each continuous feature independently from a standard normal and converts it using the training mean and standard deviation. sample_around_instance=True changes the center to the explained value. With default discretization, it samples training-bin frequencies. Current R lime samples training-bin frequencies by default. Without binning, it uses a separate density estimate for each continuous column by default.
Categorical predictors are sampled using their training frequencies in both implementations. The generated columns are therefore generally independent conditional on the package’s marginal summaries. Relationships among predictors need not be preserved.

title: 3  How LIME works
text:
3.4 Model and interpretable representations
The original LIME framework distinguishes a model representation \(z_i\) from an interpretable representation \(z_i'\). The black box receives \(z_i\). The surrogate receives \(z_i'\).
For a numerical tabular model, both representations may contain the same continuous measurements. With discretization, however, a measured biomarker value in \(z_i\) can become an indicator in \(z_i'\) such as
\[z_{ij}' =
\begin{cases}
1, & \text{if biomarker A is in the interval }(0.6,1.4],\\
0, & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}\]
For text, an element of \(z_i'\) can indicate whether a word is present. For an image, it can indicate whether a superpixel is visible. The distinction allows the fitted model to use the representation it requires while the explanation uses features a person can read.
The rest of the main derivation writes \(z_i\) for the surrogate input to keep the notation light. If a separate interpretable representation is used, every occurrence of \(z_i\) in the surrogate design matrix should be read as \(z_i'\) instead.

title: 3  How LIME works
text:
3.5 Distance defines the neighborhood
For every perturbation, calculate a distance from the explained observation,
\[d(x_0,z_i).\]
Raw Euclidean distance is
\[d(x_0,z_i)
=
\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^p (x_{0j}-z_{ij})^2}.\]
This expression is dominated by features with large numerical scales. An age measured in years can vary by tens while a normalized gene-expression value varies by one or two. The units, rather than the model’s local behaviour, would determine what counts as nearby.
For continuous features, a common correction is to standardize each difference using a training-set scale \(s_j\):
\[d_{\mathrm{scaled}}(x_0,z_i)
=
\sqrt{
\sum_{j=1}^p
\left(
\frac{x_{0j}-z_{ij}}{s_j}
\right)^2
}.\]
Python tabular LIME uses standardized interpretable data before its default Euclidean distance. A categorical feature is represented as one when it matches the explained value and zero otherwise. A discretized continuous feature is treated in the same match-versus-not-match form.
Datasets containing both numerical and categorical predictors need a distance that can combine unlike types. Gower distance calculates a feature-level dissimilarity between zero and one, scaling numerical differences by their training ranges and using match or mismatch for categorical values, then averages across available features. Current R lime uses Gower distance by default. This is an implementation choice, not part of the universal definition of LIME.

title: 3  How LIME works
text:
3.6 Distance becomes locality weight
A locality kernel turns distance into an influence weight. A useful conceptual form is
\[\pi_{x_0}(z_i)
=
\exp\left(
-\frac{d(x_0,z_i)^2}{\sigma^2}
\right),\]
where \(\sigma>0\) is the kernel width. When \(d=0\), the weight is one. The weight decreases toward zero as distance grows. A small \(\sigma\) gives appreciable weight only to close perturbations. A large \(\sigma\) lets a broader region influence the surrogate.
The released Python implementation and the non-Gower path in current R lime use
\[\pi_{x_0}(z_i)
=
\sqrt{
\exp\left(-\frac{d(x_0,z_i)^2}{\sigma^2}\right)
}
=
\exp\left(-\frac{d(x_0,z_i)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right).\]
The default Python width is
\[\sigma = 0.75\sqrt{p}.\]
For R’s default Gower path, let \(d_G\) be Gower distance and let \(q\) be gower_pow. Similarity is
\[\pi_{x_0}(z_i)=1-d_G(x_0,z_i)^q.\]
kernel_width is not used on that path. These exact formulas explain why changing the same-looking argument across languages does not necessarily create the same neighborhood.







Figure 3.1: Exponential locality weights for three kernel widths.

title: 3  How LIME works
section: 3.7 The local surrogate as weighted regression
text:
3.7 The local surrogate as weighted regression
Take a linear surrogate from a class \(G\) of interpretable models:
\[g(z_i)
=
\beta_0+\beta_1z_{i1}+\cdots+\beta_pz_{ip}.\]
The coefficients are chosen to minimize locally weighted squared error,
\[\sum_{i=1}^{m}
\pi_{x_0}(z_i)
\left[y_i^*-g(z_i)\right]^2.\]
For regression, substituting the generated response gives
\[\sum_{i=1}^{m}
\pi_{x_0}(z_i)
\left[\hat f(z_i)-g(z_i)\right]^2.\]
For classification and class \(c\), it becomes
\[\sum_{i=1}^{m}
\pi_{x_0}(z_i)
\left[\hat f_c(z_i)-g(z_i)\right]^2.\]
Each term compares a black-box output with a surrogate output on the same artificial row. Squaring prevents positive and negative errors from cancelling. Multiplying by \(\pi_{x_0}(z_i)\) makes a mistake close to \(x_0\) more costly than the same mistake far away.

title: 3  How LIME works
text:
3.8 Matrix form
Put the \(m\) surrogate inputs into a design matrix with a column of ones for the intercept:
\[Z=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & z_{11} & \cdots & z_{1p}\\
1 & z_{21} & \cdots & z_{2p}\\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots\\
1 & z_{m1} & \cdots & z_{mp}
\end{bmatrix}.\]
Collect the generated responses in
\[\mathbf y^*=
\begin{bmatrix}
\hat f(z_1)\\
\hat f(z_2)\\
\vdots\\
\hat f(z_m)
\end{bmatrix}\]
for regression, or replace \(\hat f\) with \(\hat f_c\) for classification. Put the locality weights on the diagonal of
\[W=\operatorname{diag}(w_1,w_2,\ldots,w_m),
\qquad
w_i=\pi_{x_0}(z_i).\]
The weighted objective is compactly
\[(\mathbf y^*-Z\beta)^\top W(\mathbf y^*-Z\beta).\]
Differentiating with respect to \(\beta\), setting the result to zero, and solving gives the weighted least-squares estimate
\[\hat\beta
=
(Z^\top WZ)^{-1}Z^\top W\mathbf y^*.\]
\(Z^\top WZ\) summarizes the weighted geometry of the artificial predictors. \(Z^\top W\mathbf y^*\) summarizes their weighted relationship with the black-box outputs. The inverse maps those summaries into the coefficient vector.
Ridge regression stabilizes the solution when columns are correlated or information is weak. Let
\[P=\operatorname{diag}(0,1,\ldots,1)\]
so the intercept is not penalized. The solution becomes
\[\hat\beta
=
(Z^\top WZ+\lambda P)^{-1}Z^\top W\mathbf y^*.\]
Both packages use ridge regression for the final common tabular surrogate, though their scaling and regularization details differ.

title: 3  How LIME works
text:
3.9 Explanation complexity and feature selection
A local model using all \(p\) features may be faithful but not interpretable. The general LIME objective expresses both requirements:
\[\xi(x_0)
=
\arg\min_{g\in G}
\mathcal L(\hat f,g,\pi_{x_0})
+
\Omega(g).\]
Every component has now been constructed. \(x_0\) is the observation being explained. \(G\) is the class of permitted interpretable models. \(\mathcal L\) is the loss measuring how poorly \(g\) reproduces \(\hat f\) under locality weights \(\pi_{x_0}\). \(\Omega(g)\) measures or constrains explanation complexity. \(\xi(x_0)\) is the selected explanation.
Packages commonly implement complexity by requesting at most \(K\) features and choosing them before the final ridge fit. The practical strategies include:

Forward selection. Start empty and add the feature that most improves weighted regression fit at each step.
Highest weights. Fit a ridge model using all features and retain features with the largest weighted coefficient criterion.
Lasso path. Follow a sparse regression path and choose features that persist as regularization changes.
No selection. Use every feature and ignore the requested maximum.

The auto setting in both packages uses forward selection when \(K\leq6\) and a highest-weights strategy when \(K>6\). R also offers a tree-based selection option. These are algorithms for constructing a sparse approximation to the general objective. They are not mathematically identical ways of solving one fixed penalty.

title: 3  How LIME works
section: 3.11 Linear regression can approximate probability output
text:
3.11 Linear regression can approximate probability output
The black-box function \(\hat f_c(z)\) can be nonlinear while
\[\hat f_c(z)\approx g(z)\]
holds in a weighted neighborhood. LIME never requires
\[\hat f_c(z)=g(z)\]
over the full predictor space.
A linear surrogate can produce values below zero or above one if evaluated far from its fitting neighborhood. This does not make it a calibrated probability model. It is an explanatory approximation that should not be used as a replacement classifier. Ordinary logistic regression is not required because the training targets of the surrogate are continuous probabilities, not binary outcomes.

title: 3  How LIME works
section: 3.12 The surrogate is not a Taylor approximation
text:
3.12 The surrogate is not a Taylor approximation
A local line can resemble a tangent, but ordinary LIME does not compute the gradient of \(\hat f\) at \(x_0\). It samples a neighborhood, evaluates the fitted model, weights rows by proximity, selects features, and estimates a regression. Its coefficients depend on the sampled distribution and kernel, not only on derivatives at one point.
This distinction matters for random forests and boosted trees. Their prediction surfaces are piecewise constant and may not have a conventional smooth derivative at a split. LIME can still fit a surrogate across nearby sampled regions.

title: 3  How LIME works
text:
3.13 Local fidelity
Define the weighted mean of the generated responses as
\[\bar y_w^*
=
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i y_i^*}{\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i}.\]
A weighted local coefficient of determination is
\[R^2_{\mathrm{local}}
=
1-
\frac{
\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i[y_i^*-g(z_i)]^2
}{
\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i[y_i^*-\bar y_w^*]^2
}.\]
The numerator is the surrogate’s weighted squared error. The denominator is the weighted error from predicting the same constant for every perturbation. Values near one indicate that the surrogate reproduces most of the local variation. A value near zero means it is little better than the weighted mean. A negative value is possible when it is worse.
model_r2 in R and score in the released Python package report the local regression’s weighted \(R^2\). They are in-sample measures on artificial observations. They assess approximation within the generated neighborhood, not predictive accuracy on real held-out outcomes.
Two checks complement each other:
\[R^2_{\mathrm{local}}\]
assesses the neighborhood as a whole, while
\[|g(x_0)-\hat f_c(x_0)|\]
checks the surrogate specifically at the observation being explained. A good explanation should not ignore either.

title: 3  How LIME works
text:
3.14 Kernel width changes the estimand
Suppose three widths are used with the same black box and \(x_0\):
\[\sigma_1<\sigma_2<\sigma_3.\]
They produce three different weight matrices,
\[W^{(1)},W^{(2)},W^{(3)},\]
and therefore three coefficient estimates,
\[\hat\beta^{(k)}
=
(Z^\top W^{(k)}Z+\lambda P)^{-1}
Z^\top W^{(k)}\mathbf y^*.\]
The coefficient can change magnitude or sign because each width emphasizes a different part of a nonlinear surface. This is more than a software nuisance. The meaning of local is part of the question being answered. A narrow width can also produce a small effective sample size, making the fit unstable. A wide width can improve numerical stability while reducing locality.

title: 3  How LIME works
text:
3.15 Sampling and instability
Random perturbation produces a different design matrix on each run,
\[Z^{(1)},Z^{(2)},Z^{(3)},\ldots\]
The black-box responses, distances, selected features, and fitted coefficients consequently change:
\[\hat\beta^{(1)},\hat\beta^{(2)},\hat\beta^{(3)},\ldots\]
Increasing \(m\) usually reduces this Monte Carlo variation. Setting a seed selects one reproducible \(Z^{(r)}\). It does not show that another plausible perturbation sample would give the same explanation. Stability is assessed by repeating the complete process and comparing selected features, signs, magnitudes, local predictions, and fidelity.

title: 3  How LIME works
section: 3.16 Correlated predictors and the data manifold
text:
3.16 Correlated predictors and the data manifold
Suppose two biomarkers satisfy approximately
\[X_2=X_1+\varepsilon,\]
where \(\varepsilon\) is small. Observed rows occupy a narrow band. If the perturbation scheme samples the two columns independently, it generates combinations with high \(X_1\) and low \(X_2\), or the reverse, even though these combinations were absent from training.







Figure 3.3: Independent perturbations leave the narrow manifold occupied by two correlated biomarkers.




The black box is then evaluated where it has little empirical support. The resulting responses \(\hat f(z_i)\) can reflect arbitrary extrapolation. At the same time, columns of \(Z\) are nearly redundant in plausible regions. Several coefficient vectors can give similar predictions, and sparse selection may alternate between the two biomarkers.
A conditional perturbation generator can keep samples closer to the joint distribution, but it changes the explanation procedure and requires another model for that distribution. Grouping related predictors changes the unit of explanation. Neither choice is neutral. The important point is to state the neighborhood actually used and test its consequences.

title: 3  How LIME works
text:
3.17 High-dimensional data
When \(p\) is large, several parts of the construction become difficult.
First, Euclidean distances tend to concentrate. In many high-dimensional distributions, the difference between typical near and far distances becomes small relative to the mean distance. A kernel then has difficulty separating clearly local from distant rows.
Second, biological predictors are often strongly correlated. Independent marginal perturbation moves increasingly far from the joint data manifold as more coordinates are changed.
Third, selecting \(K\) features from thousands becomes a variable-selection problem with substantial sampling variability. A short list may look decisive even when many correlated lists fit almost equally well.
Fourth, computation grows. Each of \(m\) perturbations must be transformed and passed through \(\hat f\), and feature selection may repeatedly fit weighted models.
These points do not prove that LIME is invalid when \(p\) is large. They imply that distance, perturbation plausibility, feature grouping, representation, stability, and fidelity need explicit investigation. Explaining pathway scores or fitted latent components can be more stable than explaining thousands of raw genes, but the biological meaning then belongs to those transformed features.

title: 3  How LIME works
section: 3.18 What is linear and what can remain nonlinear
text:
3.18 What is linear and what can remain nonlinear
Three objects should remain separate:

The biological data-generating process may be linear or nonlinear.
The fitted black-box model \(\hat f\) may be linear or nonlinear.
LIME is a framework for fitting an interpretable local surrogate. Common tabular implementations use a linear ridge surrogate.

A nonlinear XGBoost classifier can therefore have a linear LIME explanation for one observation. The linearity applies to \(g\) in the selected representation and weighted neighborhood. It says nothing by itself about the global fitted model or the biological system.

title: 3  How LIME works
text:
3.19 The complete algorithm
For one observation \(x_0\) and, in classification, one class \(c\):

Generate \(m\) artificial observations \(z_i\) from summaries of the training predictors.
Convert them to interpretable representations \(z_i'\) when required.
Evaluate the fitted model to obtain \(y_i^*=\hat f(z_i)\) or \(y_i^*=\hat f_c(z_i)\).
Calculate distances \(d(x_0,z_i)\) in the chosen representation and scale.
Convert distances into locality weights \(w_i=\pi_{x_0}(z_i)\).
Select a small set of interpretable features.
Fit a weighted local ridge regression of \(y_i^*\) on the selected columns of \(z_i'\).
Report the coefficients, local prediction, and fidelity diagnostics.

The method is simple enough to summarize in eight steps. Its interpretation still depends on the choices inside each step. That dependence is the reason the practical chapter treated tuning, stability, and plausibility as part of the explanation rather than optional refinements.
